The central question is: when you take a vision-language model (VLM) whose power comes from learned correspondences between visual and linguistic representations, and then fine-tune it heavily on a task that uses only one modality — say, pure text instruction-following or image classification without captions — do those cross-modal correspondences degrade, and if so, how and why? The key concepts are representational alignment (the geometry of how image embeddings and text embeddings are positioned relative to each other in shared or bridged latent spaces), fine-tuning induced drift (gradient updates shifting representations to optimize the new objective, potentially at the cost of prior structure), and catastrophic forgetting at the representational rather than just behavioral level. Beginners worry about whether benchmark accuracy drops; experts worry about something subtler — that behavioral performance on held-out multimodal tasks can remain superficially intact while the underlying representational geometry has quietly collapsed, meaning the model is solving problems through a different, more brittle mechanism than before. The expert also recognizes that alignment isn't a single scalar property: you can lose semantic alignment (a dog image no longer neighbors the word "dog") while retaining compositional alignment or vice versa, so coarse probes miss the damage entirely. Finally, the architecture matters enormously — whether the vision and language towers share parameters, are bridged by a cross-attention mechanism, or are fused via a learned projector (like a Q-Former or a linear adapter) determines which parts of the geometry are exposed to gradient flow during unimodal fine-tuning and thus where collapse is most likely to initiate.

Cross-modal nearest-neighbor consistency is almost certainly the most fragile property, because it depends on a delicate global constraint — that the neighborhood of an image embedding in the joint space is populated by semantically related text embeddings — while unimodal fine-tuning only rewards intra-modal objectives that are entirely indifferent to this constraint. Empirically, work on CLIP fine-tuning (e.g., Wortsman et al.'s "model soups" and the WiSE-FT line) shows that even modest fine-tuning on vision-only distributions shifts image encoder weights enough to break retrieval consistency at roughly 10–20% of fine-tuning steps before any accuracy drop is detectable on vision benchmarks. Isotropy is secondarily vulnerable but in a directional way: pre-training via contrastive objectives (CLIP, ALIGN) tends to produce moderately isotropic unimodal subspaces specifically because the loss penalizes representational collapse within each modality, but unimodal fine-tuning reintroduces anisotropy by amplifying task-relevant directions — effectively rotating and stretching the embedding space so that the projector or bridge layer, which was calibrated to a specific geometric relationship between modalities, is now pointing at the wrong subspace. The neighborhood structure within each modality is more robust because it is partially reinforced by the fine-tuning task itself (similar images still neighbor each other), which is why behavioral probes that measure unimodal retrieval can give false reassurance. What's especially insidious about the cross-modal nearest-neighbor collapse is that it's asymmetric: fine-tuning the vision tower while freezing the language tower (common in systems like LLaVA-style architectures) causes image embeddings to drift while text embeddings stay fixed, so the damage shows up entirely on the image→text retrieval direction and is invisible to text→text evaluations that dominate standard benchmarks. The projector or adapter layer cannot compensate for this drift because it too is either frozen or under-constrained during unimodal fine-tuning — it was trained to bridge a specific geometric configuration that no longer exists.

The projector can serve as a corrective only when two conditions hold simultaneously: the unimodal fine-tuning task provides gradient signal that flows through the projector in a way that preserves the semantic structure the language tower expects, and the projector has sufficient capacity and is not so over-parameterized that it simply absorbs the drift as a coordinate change without any semantic regularization. In practice, linear projectors (as in the original LLaVA) are the most dangerous case — they have just enough freedom to remap drifted image embeddings into the language tower's input space in a way that looks locally consistent but destroys the compositionality of the original alignment, because a linear map can compensate for rigid rotations and scalings of the vision encoder's output while being completely blind to the nonlinear neighborhood distortions that carry semantic content. Q-Former style projectors (BLIP-2, InstructBLIP) are theoretically more robust because the cross-attention mechanism forces the projector to actively query specific semantic content from the vision encoder rather than passively remap its outputs — but this advantage evaporates if the query tokens themselves overfit to the unimodal fine-tuning distribution, which Dai et al.'s InstructBLIP ablations hint at when instruction-tuning is applied without visual diversity in the training mix. The amplification failure mode occurs when the projector is trained on a unimodal task that has an implicit low-rank signal — for instance, pure text generation where visual features are largely ignored — because the projector's gradient will push it toward a solution that maps any visual input to a small region of language space that is sufficient for the task, effectively collapsing the visual input distribution at the language interface even if the vision encoder itself hasn't drifted much. Empirically, the closest evidence comes from the "visual instruction tuning" literature showing that models fine-tuned on text-heavy VQA tasks without sufficient visual grounding develop what amounts to a texture-insensitive projector — they perform well on language-dominant benchmarks while catastrophically failing on tasks requiring fine-grained visual discrimination (MMBench visual grounding subtasks drop 15–25% in such regimes). The corrective scenario most reliably occurs when the fine-tuning data includes contrastive or ranking structure that happens to reinforce cross-modal alignment — essentially smuggling in alignment signal through the task structure — which is why instruction-tuning mixtures that include image-caption pairs alongside task data (as in LLaVA-1.5's training mix) show markedly less collapse than pure task fine-tuning.

The most sensitive geometric signature is cross-modal rank consistency: for a probe set of image-caption pairs, measure whether the rank of the correct caption among text nearest-neighbors of the image embedding is preserved before and after fine-tuning, specifically tracking the distribution of rank shifts rather than mean recall@k, because early-stage collapse shows up as heavy-tailed rank degradation — a small fraction of concepts losing alignment catastrophically — while the mean stays stable and recall@1 barely moves. A second necessary measurement is cross-modal isotropy divergence: compute the ratio of singular value spectra of the image-to-text alignment matrix before and after fine-tuning, since collapse preferentially kills the lower singular values that carry compositional and relational content while preserving the top components that handle dominant visual categories, meaning standard retrieval metrics which are dominated by top-singular-value directions give false reassurance. Behaviorally, the sharpest early-warning probe is negation sensitivity in cross-modal retrieval — testing whether the model correctly ranks "a dog chasing a cat" above "a cat chasing a dog" for a given image, because this requires the alignment geometry to preserve relational structure, not just object co-occurrence, and this degrades roughly 2–3x faster than object-level retrieval under unimodal fine-tuning (suggested by compositional retrieval benchmarks like CREPE and SugarCrepe where fine-tuned models drop 20–30% on hard negatives while losing only 2–5% on standard recall). A fourth signature is mutual information between intermediate-layer representations across modalities, measurable via MINE or CKA: Raghu et al.-style CKA analysis applied cross-modally would show inter-layer alignment collapsing in middle layers — where semantic grounding happens — before it appears in final-layer metrics that benchmarks actually probe. Critically, the diagnostic suite needs a temporal component — measurements taken at fixed fine-tuning step intervals — because the collapse dynamics matter: a suite that only measures before and after misses the finding that cross-modal nearest-neighbor consistency often partially recovers late in fine-tuning through implicit regularization, creating a false impression of robustness that masks the intermediate representational damage which may have already corrupted the projector's calibration.

The most direct intervention would be a spectral regularization term added to the unimodal fine-tuning loss that penalizes deviation of the lower singular values of the cross-modal alignment matrix from their pre-training values — concretely, something like a weighted Frobenius penalty on the difference between current and reference alignment matrices, with weights inversely proportional to singular value magnitude so that small singular values (compositional directions) are protected more aggressively than large ones. This is related to but distinct from EWC (elastic weight consolidation), which operates in parameter space rather than representation space; the key advantage of working directly on the alignment matrix is that it is architecture-agnostic and can be computed on a small frozen probe set of image-caption pairs without requiring the full pre-training data, making it practically feasible in a way that replay-based methods often aren't. A partial empirical precedent exists in the "tangent space" fine-tuning literature — work by Ilharco et al. on task arithmetic and by Guillermo Ortiz-Jimenez on the geometry of fine-tuning shows that constraining weight updates to lie in subspaces that preserve pre-trained feature structure reduces forgetting, and the singular value framing is essentially making this constraint explicit in representation space rather than weight space. The first failure mode is computational: the cross-modal alignment matrix for a model like CLIP-ViT-L requires maintaining and differentiating through an SVD at each training step, which is O(min(d_v, d_t)²·max(d_v, d_t)) per batch and becomes prohibitive unless approximated via randomized SVD or a low-rank proxy — and those approximations preferentially capture large singular values, defeating the purpose of protecting small ones. The second and more fundamental failure mode is that the lower singular value directions identified at pre-training initialization may not be the correct ones to preserve after even a small amount of legitimate task adaptation: if the unimodal task genuinely requires remapping some compositional directions, the regularizer becomes an adversary to learning rather than a safeguard, and there is currently no principled way to distinguish "compositional directions worth preserving" from "compositional directions that happened to encode pre-training distribution artifacts that the new task should override." A third failure mode specific to asymmetric architectures (frozen language tower, trainable vision encoder) is that regularizing the alignment matrix penalizes vision encoder drift but cannot prevent the projector from compensating in ways that look geometrically compliant while destroying semantic fidelity — the regularizer measures a global matrix property that a sufficiently flexible projector can game locally.

The cleanest empirical test for genuine compositionality versus artifact is cross-dataset consistency of directional semantics: a singular value direction that encodes real compositional structure should activate predictably for the same semantic relationship (e.g., spatial prepositions, negation, attribute binding) across image-caption pairs drawn from visually and linguistically distinct distributions — Winoground, CREPE, and ARO each stress different compositional axes — whereas artifact directions will show high within-distribution activation but near-random cross-dataset consistency, because they are encoding corpus-specific co-occurrence patterns rather than abstract relational structure. A second test exploits the known scaling behavior of signal versus noise in empirical covariance matrices: random matrix theory (specifically the Marchenko-Pastur distribution) predicts the bulk eigenvalue spectrum you'd expect from finite-sample noise given your dataset size and embedding dimension, and singular value directions that fall within the bulk are statistically indistinguishable from noise regardless of their apparent semantic loading, while directions significantly above the bulk edge have at least passed the threshold of being data-supported — for CLIP trained on 400M pairs with embedding dimension 768, this bulk edge falls around singular values that correspond to roughly the top 40–60 directions, suggesting the bottom several hundred are in a genuinely ambiguous regime. A more direct probe is interventional: systematically zero out specific singular value directions in the alignment matrix and measure the resulting drop on compositional benchmarks versus object-recognition benchmarks — genuine compositional directions will show asymmetric damage (large compositional drop, small recognition drop), while artifact directions will show either uniform small effects or damage only on narrow distributional quirks of the pre-training data. The distinction absolutely changes what the regularizer should protect: directions that are both above the Marchenko-Pastur bulk edge and show cross-dataset compositional consistency are high-confidence targets for regularization; directions below the bulk edge should arguably be excluded from regularization or even actively allowed to drift, since protecting statistically noisy directions may be actively harmful by anchoring the model to pre-training sampling artifacts that the fine-tuning task could otherwise correct. The hard empirical case is the middle regime — directions just above the bulk edge that show moderate cross-dataset consistency — and here the honest answer is that current methods cannot reliably separate signal from structured noise without ground-truth compositional annotations that are expensive to collect at the scale needed to cover the full semantic range encoded in a model like CLIP or BLIP-2.

An unsupervised approach is theoretically sound but only if the alignment matrix contains geometric structure that reliably co-varies with compositionality — and there is a credible candidate: compositional directions should exhibit higher cross-modal symmetry than artifact directions, meaning the singular vectors on the image side and text side of the alignment matrix should be more mutually predictable for compositional dimensions than for co-occurrence artifact dimensions, because genuine compositionality by definition encodes the same abstract relationship in both modalities rather than reflecting one modality's distributional quirks. The specific structure to exploit is the block behavior of the alignment matrix under semantic perturbation: if you construct paired perturbation sets — image pairs that differ only in a single relational attribute, and caption pairs that differ correspondingly — compositional directions are precisely those whose singular vectors respond consistently to matched perturbations across modalities, while artifact directions respond to one modality's perturbation but not the other's, and this can be detected without labels by measuring the correlation between image-side and text-side activation changes under a library of unsupervised augmentations. A related geometric signature is linearity of interpolation: genuine compositional directions should support approximately linear traversal in the alignment space — the midpoint between "dog left of cat" and "cat left of dog" embeddings should land near a semantically neutral "dog and cat" embedding — whereas artifact directions will show nonlinear or semantically incoherent interpolation behavior, a property measurable purely from the geometry without behavioral labels and related to the linear representation hypothesis work by Elhage et al. and the concept arithmetic findings in CLIP by Goh et al. The theoretical soundness concern is that these geometric signatures are necessary but not sufficient conditions for compositionality: a direction could exhibit high cross-modal symmetry and linear interpolation simply because it encodes a very frequent co-occurrence pattern that happens to appear consistently in both modalities, and without some external semantic anchor there is no way to distinguish "frequent symmetric co-occurrence" from "genuine compositional structure" purely from matrix geometry.
